source: Watkins & Watkins (1975) Buildup of proactive inhibition as a cue-overload effect (JEP:HLM 1:442-452)
finding: Founding statement of cue overload: a retrieval cue becomes less effective the more items are filed under it. Applied to buildup of proactive inhibition in short-term recall: later trials fail because the same cue now points to more items.
numbers: Not read this session; only the citation and one-line definitions seen in search results and in Schneider and Anderson (2012). Experiment sizes and recall figures are NOT recorded here.
limits: Original paper inaccessible by tools; verify before quoting any number.
agent_relevance: Names the mechanism for a scaffold: the size of the item set under one cue (library size per cue) is what hurts retrieval, not age or time.

source: Anderson (1974) Retrieval of propositional information from long-term memory (Cognitive Psychology 6:451-474)
finding: Founding fan experiments. People learned person-location sentences (A hippie is in the park) and then judged whether probes were studied. Probe time rose with the number of facts attached to the person or the location.
numbers: Wikipedia (a20) and Anderson (1983) describe 3 experiments with 26 study sentences. Exact 1974 reaction times were not read.
limits: Original not opened (publisher paywall). The description comes from secondary pages that I did read (a03, a20).
agent_relevance: The fan paradigm is a ready-made test: one cue, N attached facts, measure accuracy and latency.

source: Anderson (1983) Retrieval of information from long-term memory (Science 220:25-30)
finding: Fan paradigm defined: subjects memorize 26 person-location sentences, are drilled to perfect recall, then verify probes. Fan of a concept is the number of facts linked to it (1 to 3). Reaction time rises with the fan of the person AND of the location, for targets and foils.
numbers: Targets are verified faster than foils by about 100 ms. Extracted Table 1 cells run from 1.169 s (lowest target cell) to 1.465 s (highest foil cell); column means 1.204 s (targets) and 1.308 s (foils) as extracted. Errors low and mostly speed-stress slips.
quote: A fan of two is associated with each.
limits: Table text was garbled by PDF extraction, so cell-to-condition mapping is approximate. Review, not the original data.
agent_relevance: Both cue terms in a query contribute. A query built from two high-fan terms is slowest.

source: Anderson (1983) Retrieval of information from long-term memory (Science 220:25-30)
finding: Limited-capacity spreading activation: each concept has a fixed capacity to spread activation. More links out of a concept means less activation down any one link, so the fact reaches threshold later. Activation spreads in parallel from every concept in the probe.
numbers: Contrast model tested: access from only one probe concept (e.g. the first). That predicts fan effects of one concept only. Data show roughly equal effects of both, so the parallel model is favoured.
limits: Later ACT-R versions dropped multi-link spread and use direct source-to-chunk activation (a14).
agent_relevance: Gives the quantitative reason a big library per cue is slow and error prone: a fixed attention budget is divided over links.

source: Anderson (1983) Retrieval of information from long-term memory (Science 220:25-30)
finding: Foils are rejected by a waiting process: the system waits a set time for activation to intersect and says no if none does. Wait is longer when the probe concepts have higher fan, so foils show a fan effect too.
numbers: King and Anderson test: connected sentence pairs sharing a subject. Targets: no difference connected versus unconnected. Foils: much slower and more errors when connected, because the shared subject creates a spurious intersection.
limits: Based on summaries of earlier experiments (refs 5, 7 in the review), not the originals.
agent_relevance: A near-match in the library (shared subject) raises false accepts. Verification steps must check the whole fact, not one shared cue.

source: Anderson (1983) Retrieval of information from long-term memory (Science 220:25-30)
finding: Relative strength, not raw count, drives the effect. With equal study frequency, a 2-fan fact and a 4-fan fact differ little. With equal fan, a fact studied 3 times beats one studied once by a lot.
numbers: Example design: 2-fan facts each f=3; 4-fan facts f=3,1,1,1. Unpublished result: a 2-fan fact studied 4 times is slower when its sibling was studied 8 times than 2 times. In a normal fan study strength share is 1/N.
limits: Frequency result partly unpublished in this review.
agent_relevance: Strengthening one item (repeat, rehearse, tag as important) protects it from a crowded cue. Equal weighting of N items does not.

source: Anderson (1983) Retrieval of information from long-term memory (Science 220:25-30)
finding: Practice removes the fan effect. Over 25 days (5 per week for 5 weeks), 24 test presentations a day, about 600 per sentence, recognition time fell as a power law toward the same asymptote for fan and no-fan sentences.
numbers: No-fan fit: T = 0.36 + 1.15 P^-0.51 (seconds, P days). Fan and no-fan have the same exponent and same asymptote 0.36 s, so the effect would vanish with enough practice. 8 sentences per condition, learned to perfect recall first.
limits: Small design (8 sentences per condition), exact fan-condition coefficients lost in extraction.
agent_relevance: Well-practiced cues tolerate large libraries. A well-rehearsed, proceduralized lookup should not need pruning; novel ones should.

source: Anderson (1983) Retrieval of information from long-term memory (Science 220:25-30)
finding: The fan effect appears with real-world knowledge, faces and many materials. Lewis and Anderson: learning new fantasy facts about a famous person slowed retrieval of old true facts about that person. Faces: fan 1-1, 3-1, 3-3 gave slower recognition as features were shared by more faces.
numbers: Familiar vs less familiar senators: 2.16 s (Kennedy) vs 2.50 s (Bayh), uncontrolled. Later controlled work reported as giving the same result.
limits: Paradox of the expert: more knowledge should slow retrieval but experts often are faster. Anderson attributes this to practice and organisation.
agent_relevance: Adding new facts to an old cue can slow retrieval of old facts. Memory writes by the agent are not free for the cues they touch.

source: Anderson (1983) Retrieval of information from long-term memory (Science 220:25-30)
finding: Boundary condition: no fan effect when the facts can be integrated into one theme and the foils are unrelated. Smith et al.: Marty 2 facts vs 2 plus an integrated third fact gave no difference, while a third unrelated fact slowed responses. Reder and Anderson: the fan effect returns when foils are related, because then a consistency judgment is not enough.
numbers: Reder and Anderson: two themes about one person slow judgments versus one theme, but the number of facts in the irrelevant theme did not matter (relevant fan only).
limits: Summary of earlier work; effect size not given in the review.
agent_relevance: Grouping library items under sub-cues (themes) cuts the effective fan. Structure the library, do not enlarge a flat list.

source: Schneider & Anderson (2012) Modeling fan effects on the time course of associative recognition (Cogn Psychol)
finding: Standard ACT-R fan model written out. Chunk activation A = B + sum of W_j S_ji. Association S_ji = S - ln(fan_j), so doubling fan lowers each link by ln 2. Retrieval time = F e^-A. Source activation W is split equally over sources. Foils are rejected by recall-to-reject: retrieve the best chunk, compare, say no on mismatch.
numbers: Equations 1-3 and 2b. Extension: failure time F e^-threshold gives an internal deadline, so lower activation lowers the probability of finishing in time.
quote: Associative activation reflects the strength of association between chunks in declarative memory
limits: Mean RT model; the paper extends it to response-signal accuracy.
agent_relevance: A concrete formula for library cost per cue: strength falls with the log of the count, so cost grows slowly but without bound.

source: Schneider & Anderson (2012) Modeling fan effects on the time course of associative recognition (Cogn Psychol)
finding: New response-signal experiment with well-learned facts: fan lowered the asymptote or the rate of rise of accuracy, or both. Fan 1 beat Fan 2 mostly at intermediate lags and the gap closed at the longest lag.
numbers: N=10 CMU subjects, 5 daily sessions (first 2 h, rest 1 h). 32 person-location facts, half fan 1 and half fan 2, from 24 persons and 24 locations. Trials with signal lag RT under 100 ms or over 350 ms dropped (5.7%). Accuracy near chance at the shortest lag.
limits: Only 10 subjects. Fan levels 1 and 2 only.
agent_relevance: Time pressure turns fan into errors, not just delay. A fixed token or step budget may do the same to a crowded cue.

source: Schneider & Anderson (2012) Modeling fan effects on the time course of associative recognition (Cogn Psychol)
finding: ACT-R fit as good as the best descriptive model (shifted exponential). Earlier response-signal studies (Wickelgren and Corbett 1977; Dosher 1981) found fan changes the asymptote plus one of rate or intercept, which ACT-R reads as weaker association strength.
numbers: Fit to Wickelgren and Corbett d-prime data: mean adjusted R2 = .921 individual, .981 group. Dosher design: A-B, D-E, A-C versus no shared word, 3 s per pair.
limits: Fit with a few parameters per subject; small data sets.
agent_relevance: Supports a strength-reduction account over a pure serial-search account.

source: Schneider & Anderson (2012) Modeling fan effects on the time course of associative recognition (Cogn Psychol)
finding: States the field consensus: fan effects hold for fictional facts, real-world knowledge, faces and alphabet-arithmetic, in RT, accuracy and imaging, and fan is the same idea as cue overload (Watkins and Watkins 1975; Surprenant and Neath 2009). Accuracy cost is mainly more false alarms; hit rates are mixed.
numbers: Cited: hit-rate effects mixed (Dyne, Humphreys, Bain and Pike 1990; Verde 2004).
quote: consistent with the general principle of cue overload
limits: Hit rates are not a clean fan effect, so measure false accepts too.
agent_relevance: Track false positives, not only misses, when the library per cue grows.

source: Anderson, Reder & Lebiere (1996) Working memory: activation limitations on retrieval (Cogn Psychol 30:221-256)
finding: Working-memory limit located in retrieval: a fixed total of source activation, sum of W_j = constant, is shared by all cues in focus. More concurrent load leaves less activation per cue, so odds and speed of retrieval drop. Odds = C e^(cA); time = B e^(-bA).
numbers: Two experiments: digit span held while solving an equation. Harder either task hurt both. Experiment 1 had 15 subjects. Most errors were misretrievals of similar active chunks. ACT-R fit with a source-activation limit; a separate-capacity model fit worse with more parameters.
limits: Equation-solving task, not a fan paradigm. The source activation scale is not identified by the data (footnote 5).
agent_relevance: Context load and cue overload are one budget in this theory: stuffing the prompt with other goals starves each cue.

source: Sohn, Anderson, Reder & Goode (2004) Differential fan effect and attentional focus (Psychon Bull Rev 11:729-734)
finding: Test of ACT-R against mental-model theory. Attention was directed to the person dimension or the location dimension. The focused dimension showed the larger fan effect, as ACT-R predicts (higher attention weight W_j) and against the mental-model prediction.
numbers: N=19 person-focus, 17 location-focus. 28 study sentences, 168 targets and 168 foils, fans 1-3. Person-focus slope: person 98 ms per fan step vs location 63 ms. Focused fan F(2,68)=56.80 (latency), nonfocused fan F(2,68)=30.91. Person-focus targets (nonfocused fan 1): 1110, 1184, 1298 ms for focused fan 1, 2, 3.
limits: Undergraduates; the photograph or grid manipulation may alter more than attention. Contradicts, not refutes, Radvansky and Zacks 1991.
agent_relevance: Cue weight can be set by the scaffold: giving one cue more weight makes its crowd matter more, so pick the discriminating cue and keep its fan low.

source: Radvansky & Zacks (2005) Age and inhibition: the retrieval of situation models (J Gerontol B 60:P276; data from Radvansky, Zacks & Hasher 1996)
finding: Mental-model counter-theory: facts that fit one situation (many objects in one location) show no fan effect; one object in several locations needs several models and shows fan. Replicated in young adults, with a much larger effect in older adults.
numbers: 32 young, 32 old, 18 sentences. Young RT multiple-location: 1441, 1615, 1853 ms for 1, 2, 3 associations; single-location 1395, 1448, 1415. Old multiple-location: 1833, 1975, 3209 ms (errors 3.9, 9.3, 18.5%); old single-location 1811, 1772, 1867. Condition x interference F(2,124)=22.5.
limits: Young adults also show inhibition: 1875 vs 1755 ms on targets related to a just-suppressed model; old adults none. Sohn et al. (a15) dispute the mental-model reading.
agent_relevance: Cue overload is lessened by integration into one model. A library should be stored as integrated cases, not scattered single-cue facts.

source: Anderson & Reder (1999) The fan effect: new results and new theories (JEP:General 128:186-197)
finding: Review that revised the ACT-R account: the fan effect depends on association strength and attention weights, and apparent absence of fan with integrated material is explained within the same retrieval mechanism.
numbers: Not read; the PDF was an image scan with no extractable text. Claim taken from how Sohn et al. (a15) and Schneider and Anderson (a10) cite it.
limits: Do not quote numbers from this entry.
agent_relevance: Primary source for ACT-R's answer to the mental-model critique.

source: Tehan & Humphreys (1996) Cuing effects in short-term recall (Memory & Cognition 24:719-732)
finding: Boundary condition on cue overload in short-term memory: proactive interference is seen only if the interfering and target items fall under the same cue. Category-dominance effects parallel PI effects. So short-term recall is cue dependent too.
numbers: Five experiments reported; abstract page only read, no cell values.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Interference needs a shared cue, so separate cues (labels, namespaces) per sub-library remove the crowd.

source: Verde (2004) Associative interference in recognition memory: a dual-process account (Memory & Cognition 32:1273-1283)
finding: Overlapping pairs (A-B, A-D) hurt recall but have inconsistent effects on recognition. Dual-process account: interference lowers recollection and raises familiarity, so false alarms always rise but hits can rise or fall.
numbers: Three experiments, materials sentences or random nouns, associative or pair recognition. Remember hits always fell and know hits always rose with interference. Numbers not extracted.
limits: Abstract page only.
agent_relevance: Warns that a crowded library may feel familiar and cause false accepts; a recall-to-reject check is what protects.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) Fan effect
finding: Summary of the 1974 experiments: three experiments, 26 person-location sentences, probe judgments. Notes mental-model theory, ACT-R, reduced fan with unified concepts, age-related increases, and an OCD technique (association splitting) built on the fan idea.
numbers: 26 sentences, 3 experiments. Cites a systematic review of association splitting (Ching et al. 2019) for symptom reduction.
limits: Tertiary source; used only to fix the design of Anderson 1974.
agent_relevance: None directly.

source: Cao, Schooler & Zafarani (2025) Analyzing memory effects in LLMs through the lens of cognitive psychology (arXiv 2509.17138v2)
finding: LLMs show a fan effect on person-location recognition. Accuracy fell as fan rose, but only mildly. Online GPT-4 (gpt-4-0125-preview) consistently beat offline Mistral-7B-Instruct and LLaMA-3-8B; all showed the same direction.
numbers: Fan effect: 0.991 to 0.915 as fan went from 1 to 2 at list size 32. Study lists from 40 persons x 40 locations. Foils rearranged within the same fan.
limits: Recognition with the whole list in context, tiny lists (32 facts), tiny fans (1 or 2). No reaction-time analogue. One group.
agent_relevance: Fan hurts LLMs even when everything is in context, but only a few points at fan 2.

source: Cao, Schooler & Zafarani (2025) Analyzing memory effects in LLMs through the lens of cognitive psychology (arXiv 2509.17138v2)
finding: d-prime is lower for Fan 2 than Fan 1 and drops as list length grows. LLMs are position invariant (no serial position curve) and robust to nonsense words, unlike people. Recall stayed near perfect while recognition showed errors.
numbers: Seven phenomena tested over two datasets. Offline models gave hit rate 1 on the position effect.
limits: Authors claim similarity to Schneider and Anderson, but only compare Fan 1 to Fan 2.
agent_relevance: Interference is real but small at tiny sizes. The risk grows with library size per cue, tested in a23 to a25.

source: Wang & Sun (2025) Unable to forget: proactive interference reveals working memory limits in LLMs (arXiv 2506.08184v3)
finding: PI-LLM task: a stream of key-value updates, ask only for the final value of each key. Accuracy falls log-linearly toward zero as updates per key rise, across about 35 models from 0.6B to 637B parameters. Errors are earlier, overwritten values.
numbers: 46 keys, update count 3 to 400. Tracking more keys at fixed input length also gives a log-linear fall: llama4-maverick near 100% with 2 tracked keys, below 5% with 46.
limits: Synthetic key-value stream; target always at the end. Does not use natural text.
agent_relevance: Direct cue overload in LLMs: one key, many old values, and the model returns an old one. Keep one live value per key.

source: Wang & Sun (2025) Unable to forget: proactive interference reveals working memory limits in LLMs (arXiv 2506.08184v3)
finding: Three load axes (updates per key, number of keys, value length) all give a log-linear decline, so the authors infer one anti-interference resource, separate from context window length. Value length is the steepest axis.
numbers: Value length 1 to 10 words: every model under 40%. At 40 words: under 5%. Larger models degrade more slowly; context window size has no significant effect on their Interference Endurance Score.
limits: Parameter size confounded with training. IES is the authors' own metric.
agent_relevance: Short values and few concurrent keys help. Do not expect a bigger context window to fix it.

source: Wang & Sun (2025) Unable to forget: proactive interference reveals working memory limits in LLMs (arXiv 2506.08184v3)
finding: Prompt fixes barely help. Telling the model to forget, to focus on later updates, or to restate the task gave marginal gains and sometimes hurt. Only a mock question-answer reset that mimics a new turn gave a substantial gain, and accuracy still fell with update count. Chain-of-thought did not help either.
numbers: Per-key forget prompt worsened gpt-4.1-mini. Relevance meta-prompt harmful for gpt-4.1-mini. Humans plateau at high interference, LLMs keep declining (Oberauer and Vockenberg 2009 cited by the authors).
limits: Prompt variants limited to the paper's set.
agent_relevance: Fits G2 and G5: remove old values with code, do not ask the model to ignore them.

source: Gan & Sun (2025) RAG-MCP: mitigating prompt bloat in LLM tool selection (arXiv 2505.03275)
finding: Tool library size per query hurts tool choice. With all MCP descriptions in the prompt (Blank), tool selection accuracy was 13.62%. Retrieving the top one tool with a vector index gave 43.13%. A keyword prefilter gave 18.20%.
numbers: Prompt tokens 2133.84 (Blank), 1646 (keyword), 1084 (RAG-MCP). Base LLM qwen-max-0125, 20 trials, MCPBench web-search subset, registry of 4,400+ servers.
limits: Single model, 20 trials; the stress test (N from 1 to 11,100) reads success above 90% below position ~30 and mostly failure past ~100, from a heat map not a table. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Selecting a smaller candidate set per query roughly triples accuracy: filter the library per cue before the model sees it.

source: Guo, Wu & Yiu (2026) The interference gap: comparing retrieval bounds in human memory and RAG systems (arXiv 2606.28327)
finding: Signal detection model with ACT-R style log fan: d'(fan) = d0 - k ln(fan). Fits human and retrieval-system data. Slope k/sigma is 0.41 for humans, 0.67 for dense passage retrieval, 0.53 ColBERTv2, 0.44 HippoRAG. Log form beat power law (BIC difference over 15).
numbers: Humans N=112 (Prolific): accuracy 91.2, 82.4, 71.8% at fan 1, 2, 4; d' 2.84, 2.21, 1.67; Cohen d = 1.12. DPR 94.1, 76.3, 58.2, 44.7% at fan 1, 2, 4, 8. 200 entities per fan level, 800 pairs per system.
limits: Preprint; only the Human-DPR contrast has non-overlapping CIs; humans not tested at fan 8; retrievers, not LLM generators. False alarm 23.1% human vs 41.3% DPR at high competitor similarity.
agent_relevance: Gives a usable curve: accuracy falls roughly 9 to 18 points per doubling of fan in these data. Plan for a steady loss per doubling.

source: Guo, Wu & Yiu (2026) The interference gap: comparing retrieval bounds in human memory and RAG systems (arXiv 2606.28327)
finding: Adds competitor density to the model: accuracy depends on fan, mean cue similarity of competitors, and serial position. Dense retrieval is more interference sensitive than humans, tied to a missing pattern-separation or encoding-specificity mechanism (hypothesis).
numbers: Parameter recovery r = .93 to .97 over 1,000 synthetic data sets; cross-validated R2 = .91 humans, .88 DPR, .90 HippoRAG.
limits: Mechanisms are explicitly untested hypotheses.
agent_relevance: Similarity of the crowd matters as much as its size: make library items distinct on the cue dimension.
